content: Childhood constipation is a prevalent condition that imposes significant health, economic, and emotional challenges. Current treatment options, which are predominantly pharmacological, often fail to provide consistent relief and may lead to adverse effects with prolonged use. Transcutaneous electrical stimulation (TES) is a non-pharmacological intervention that is hypothesized to enhance bowel motility by modulating the nerves of the large intestine through electrical currents applied via the abdominal wall. The primary aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness and safety of TES in improving bowel function and alleviating constipation-related symptoms in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including MEDLINE, CENTRAL, EMBASE, and others, covering studies up to July 2015. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing TES to no treatment, sham TES, other nerve stimulation methods, or pharmacological/non-pharmacological treatments were considered for inclusion. Two independent reviewers evaluated the studies for inclusion, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Statistical analyses were performed to calculate risk ratios (RR) and mean differences (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE criteria. Only one eligible study from Australia, involving 46 children aged 8 to 18 years, was identified. This study had multiple reports, including unpublished data, focusing on different outcomes. However, the study exhibited unclear risks of selection bias, high risks of performance, detection, and attrition biases, and low risks of reporting bias. Due to these limitations, the evidence regarding the effects of TES on bowel movements, colonic transit, soiling symptoms, and quality of life is highly uncertain. The study reported that 16 out of 21 children in the TES group and 15 out of 21 in the sham group achieved more than three complete spontaneous bowel movements (CSBM) per week (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.53; very low-quality evidence). Colonic transit improvement was observed in 10 out of 14 children in the TES group compared to 1 out of 7 in the sham group (RR 5.00, 95% CI 0.79 to 31.63; very low-quality evidence). The mean colonic transit rate, assessed radiologically, was higher in the TES group (MD 1.05, 95% CI 0.36 to 1.74; one study, 30 participants; very low-quality evidence). However, these radiological findings may not necessarily translate into meaningful clinical improvements or increased bowel movements. Regarding soiling symptoms, 9 out of 13 children in the TES group showed improvement compared to 4 out of 12 in the sham group (RR 2.08, 95% CI 0.86 to 5.00; very low-quality evidence). Quality of life (QoL) outcomes were also uncertain, with 4 out of 8 TES participants reporting improvement compared to 1 out of 8 in the sham group (RR 4.00, 95% CI 0.56 to 28.40; very low-quality evidence). Self-perceived QoL (MD 5.00, 95% CI -1.21 to 11.21; one study, 33 participants; very low-quality evidence) and parent-perceived QoL (MD -0.20, 95% CI -7.57 to 7.17; one study, 33 participants; very low-quality evidence) also showed no conclusive results. Importantly, no adverse effects were reported in the included study. In conclusion, the evidence regarding the efficacy and safety of TES for managing chronic constipation in children is highly uncertain. No definitive conclusions can be drawn from the available data. Further well-designed RCTs are necessary to evaluate TES, with a focus on robust methodologies, effective blinding, and patient-centered outcomes such as CSBM frequency, clinical symptom improvement, and quality of life.
